September 2021Torreys Peak, Colorado

Torreys Peak, CO

memories below

Higher Ground

I started up Torreys Peak around sunrise, with the valley still in shadow and only the ridgetops catching the light. It was the third week of September, and the high country was already rust and gold. Torreys is a 14,267-foot fourteener near Georgetown, and it shares a saddle with its slightly taller neighbor, Grays, which is why the two are so often climbed together. A creek ran beside the trail through yellow willows and dark spruce. Farther up, the willows gave way to tundra, and the trail led into a huge bowl of rock still sitting in shadow.

Above the saddle the trail turns steep and loose. At 14,000 feet there is about 40 percent less oxygen than at sea level, so you climb in short bursts, and every pause rewards you with a wider view. At the top the sky was a deep, clean blue with only thin bands of cloud along the horizon. A basin of gold and rust lay far below, faint trails threading across its slope. I stayed a while. A botanist gave these mountains their names. In 1861 Charles Parry made the first recorded climbs and named the peaks for two fellow botanists, Asa Gray and John Torrey. Gray didn't see his mountain until eleven years later. With this much color on the tundra, it seems fitting!

Coming down, the willows I had passed in shadow that morning were practically glowing. Same creek, same trail, and a few hours of sun had changed everything. It makes you wonder what else you walk past in the shade. The next afternoon I stopped at Loveland Pass, only a few miles from the peaks, where the highway curled through gold tundra and the ski runs across the valley lay bare, for now.
